title: UNH football rallies in final minute to beat Rhode Island - Yahoo Sports
content: DURHAM — Sophomore quarterback Tommy McLeish threw for two touchdowns and caught another to lift the University of New Hampshire football team to a 24-21 victory over the University of Rhode Island on Saturday at Wildcat Stadium. With UNH trailing 21-17 and 1:53 remaining, McLeish engineered an 11-play, 64-yard drive capped by a 1-yard touchdown pass to tight end Colby Ramshaw with 7 seconds remaining, giving the Wildcats a 24-21 lead. McLeish completed 21 of 37 passes for 271 yards and two touchdowns. He also caught a 7-yard touchdown pass from sophomore wide receiver Ryan Ricketti. Junior wide receiver Logan Perez caught four passes for 91 yards, including a 52-yard touchdown, while senior wide receiver Ja'Carree Kelly had five catches for 91 yards. Graduate student running back Myles Thomason rushed for a team-high 84 yards on 16 carries. Sophomore linebacker Trevor Barry, who entered the game leading the FCS in tackles per game, finished with 10 tackles. Graduate student safety Jackson Stone added nine tackles and an interception. Rhode Island was led by Brayden Richardson, who rushed for a game-high 138 yards, including a 64-yard touchdown. Alex McClelland completed 10 of 24 passes for 142 yards and a touchdown and added 50 rushing yards on 17 carries. New Hampshire returns to action Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m. against Stony Brook University. title: Offensive Woes Continue for River Hawks in 3-0 Home Loss to UNH - NGSC Sports
content: On Friday night, the UMass Lowell River Hawks returned home to the Tsongas Center to host the University of New Hampshire Wildcats, looking to turn around a 1-4-0 record on home ice. Sitting at 2-6-0, it marks just the fourth time in their Division I history that the River Hawks have started a season with that mark. Under head coach Norm Bazin, UML entered the night 21-19-3 against UNH. Historically, the Wildcats have won 23 all-time series against Lowell and recorded 15 shutouts overall (including eight during Bazin’s tenure). The River Hawks entered the contest following a road split at Colgate. Starting in goal for UNH was Michael Simpson, a transfer from Providence who entered the night at 3-4-1 with a 2.57 goals-against average and an .892 save percentage. The River Hawks countered with Austin Elliott (1-4-0, 4.26 GAA, .874 save percentage). A scoreless first period saw both teams struggle to generate offense. Each squad failed to capitalize on a power play, extending UMass Lowell’s streak to 16 consecutive penalty kills and 28-of-32 overall. UNH held an 11-7 advantage in shots on goal after 20 minutes. The Wildcats broke the deadlock at 1:56 of the second period when Nick Ring redirected a point shot from Malte Vass past Elliott for his fourth goal of the season, assisted by Ryan Johnson. UMass Lowell’s penalty-killing unit held strong midway through the frame, erasing two more penalties—including a 5-on-3 power play—to make it 18 straight kills and 30-of-34 overall. However, UNH extended its lead at even strength when Nick Van Tassell scored his first goal of the season from the low slot, assisted by Ryan Philbrick and Vass. The Wildcats then made it 3-0 on a power-play goal by Johnson—his second of the year—from the left side of the net at 18:41, with assists going to Ring and goaltender Simpson. UNH outshot UML 15-8 in the second period, taking a 26-15 shot advantage and a 3-0 lead into the final intermission. The River Hawks, who fell to 0-5-0 when trailing after two periods, were unable to mount a comeback in a scoreless third period. — UMass Lowell Hockey (@RiverHawkHockey) November 7, 2026 UNH netminder Michael Simpson stopped all 20 shots he faced to earn his first shutout of the season. “It’s great to get our first Hockey East win,” UNH head coach Mike Souza said after the game, adding that he liked the way his team played with the lead and noting that the penalty kill came through when needed most. On the opposing bench, Bazin was candid about his team’s performance. “Not our best effort,” Bazin said, emphasizing that the River Hawks must generate more offense both at 5-on-5 and on the power play, while signaling that line changes are coming for Saturday night’s rematch. With the result, UNH moves to 4-4-1 overall (1-2-1 Hockey East), while UMass Lowell drops to 2-7-0 overall (0-3-0 Hockey East). John is VP of NGSC Sports and head of our New England operations. title: Questions linger over UNH polling after Scott’s Vermont election win - WCAX
content:
MONTPELIER, Vt. (WCAX) - Gov. Phil Scott’s victory over Amanda Janoo in Tuesday’s election is raising questions about pre-election polling that showed him losing the Vermont governor’s race. A September poll predicted Janoo winning by six points, 49% to Scott’s 43%. A second poll, released a day before Election Day, showed Janoo ahead eight points, 51% to 43%. But it was Scott who came out on top Tuesday, beating Janoo by seven points. Polls are only accurate if the pollsters survey a representative cross-section of likely voters. The Scott team and experts say the UNH Survey Center erred in who they included in their survey. “The political pundits were writing my obituary, and the UNH poll had us losing by about nine points. It looks like we’re going to win by over five, which is a 14-point swing,” Gov. Phil Scott said on election night. It’s the third election in a row UNH has underestimated Scott’s support. “The assumptions they made about who would turn out to vote were incorrect,” said Matt Dickinson, a Middlebury College political science professor. In recent years, polling outfits have struggled to get people to pick up the phone to achieve an accurate sample. Instead, UNH and other pollsters use a preselected panel of participants to fill out the poll. Dickinson says in assembling their panels, UNH overestimated younger voter turnout, who may skew toward Janoo, and underestimated the turnout of those over 65, who may skew toward Scott. “If you incorrectly make assumptions here as UNH did, that opt-in panel can lead you astray, and that’s what happened here,” Dickinson said. “We were very accurate in every other race, except the Vermont governor’s race,” said Andy Smith, one of the lead UNH Survey Center pollsters. He says they accurately predicted Vermont’s lieutenant governor, Congress, and constitutional amendments, in addition to other races across New England. He adds the Green Mountain panel is weighted to match the distribution of people in Vermont. “The thing I think they were misleadingly looking at is saying the weight of younger people is really the weight overall of all people, adults living in Vermont, not just voters.” Smith says voters need to be cautious when interpreting the results of any poll and that pollsters around the country are grappling with the right methodology to get an accurate representation of likely voters. He says it’s too soon to tell what they will do differently next election cycle and that they will take the next few weeks to do a post-mortem of their data. Experts also say polls can influence voter behavior, such as when and how people vote or donate money to candidates, believing one candidate is ahead or behind in the race. Dickinson says that may have played a role in the Scott-Janoo race. He suspects the national Republican Governors Association wouldn’t have poured a million dollars into Vermont on behalf of Scott if the poll was conducted differently. title: Professor Kristen Johnson Receives National Innovation in Education Award - University of New Hampshire
content: Kristen Johnson, associate professor of biotechnology at the University of New Hampshire at Manchester, has received the American Society for Cell Biology’s (ASCB) 2026 Innovation in Education Award for her innovative approaches to science education and commitment to expanding research and professional development opportunities for students. Johnson was selected by an ASCB committee for her impact spanning classroom instruction, undergraduate research, industry partnerships, and national initiatives designed to make scientific learning more accessible. For Johnson, innovation in education begins with a simple idea: Students learn best when they have opportunities to experiment, make mistakes, and discover answers for themselves. That philosophy has shaped her teaching style at UNH Manchester, where she has developed research-based courses that give students hands-on experience with scientific inquiry. Rather than following prescribed experiments with predictable results, students design their own investigations, develop hypotheses, analyze data, and present their findings. Johnson has developed four distinct course-based research experiences spanning molecular biology, protein biochemistry, and cell culture. These experiences have become an integral part of the life sciences curriculum, with most students now completing at least one research-based course during their degree programs. In one molecular biology course, students previously used synthetic biology to create programmable biosensors. Today, they use freshwater flatworms to investigate human diseases. In the cell culture course, they investigate how drugs affect fat cell development to better understand metabolic diseases. These projects expose students to the challenges and discoveries of scientific research while helping them build problem-solving, collaboration, and communication skills. Johnson’s impact extends beyond the classroom. Over the past nine years, she has mentored more than 90 student researchers in her laboratory, which investigates the molecular mechanisms of pancreatic cancer and other diseases. Her approach has helped students contribute to published research, present scientific findings, and pursue advanced degrees. Johnson has also worked to expand access to biotechnology career opportunities through NH CLIMBS (Collaborative Learning through Industry Internships and Academic Mentorship in Biotech for Students), a program she developed to connect students with industry-relevant research and technologies. The initiative provided paid, hands-on research opportunities that allowed students to collaborate with biotechnology companies without having to leave campus for traditional internships. Building on this commitment to accessible, industry-relevant training, Johnson also organized summer Cell Culture Crash Course workshops for New Hampshire students whose institutions lacked access to advanced laboratory coursework. Supported by funding from NH INBRE and EPSCoR, the workshops combined technical training with industry visits, professional networking, and financial support for participants. Together, these initiatives helped reduce geographic and financial barriers to valuable research and training experiences, preparing students for opportunities in the biotechnology industry. Beyond UNH Manchester, Johnson serves as a co-principal investigator of the National Science Foundation-funded Cell Biology Education Consortium, a national initiative that helps faculty and undergraduate students publish their scientific research. Through mentorship, editorial support, and professional development programs, the consortium has supported more than 10 publications over the past two years. These efforts reflect Johnson's commitment to making meaningful scientific experiences available to students from a wide range of backgrounds, while preparing them for careers and further study in the life sciences. Johnson will be recognized at ASCB's annual Cell Bio meeting in San Diego this December, where she will deliver a presentation titled Innovation in Education: Why Uncertainty Is the Starting Point, Not the Obstacle. Drawing on her own experiences as a first-generation college student, Johnson's presentation will explore how embracing uncertainty, taking risks, and learning through trial and error can lead to more effective teaching and meaningful educational change. "Rather than viewing imperfection as something to overcome, I argue that it is the foundation of creativity, resilience, and lasting growth," Johnson writes in her presentation abstract. It's a perspective that continues to guide her work at UNH Manchester: creating opportunities for students not simply to learn about science, but to experience the process of discovery firsthand. As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. title: UNH students, faculty oppose removal of 300,000 books from library - Seacoastonline.com
content: Justin Kostopulos is not a traditional art history student at UNH. He’s 35 and a commuter, so he spends a lot of his time between classes wandering the stacks of the library. When he found out the Dimond Library was reviewing nearly 300,000 print titles for potential removal, he started a petition to ask the university to reconsider. Within a week, it gathered over 600 signatures. “Removing these texts, I think, erases decades of accrued wisdom and insight,” he said. “It deprives students the unique experience of just handling a physical book, which many times can spark curiosity and critical thinking in ways that digital media often cannot.” The book review is part of an effort by UNH to modernize its library, which was last renovated in 1996. UNH said in internal communications to staff and students that was shared with NHPR that the school was a decade overdue in going through their collections. UNH is also planning to open a new student center in the library’s unused space in a few years. UNH said their library is prioritizing digital collections to serve online students, but Kostopulos said there’s still a lot of value to keeping physical copies. “After speaking with many of my peers since starting this petition,” he said. “Many students, myself included, retain information better through physical books rather than reading something online.” The university gave faculty six weeks to review the list of potential titles, ending on Oct. 21. But some faculty, including UNH History Professor Eliga Gould, said that wasn’t enough time. As a historian, Gould also said that interests and access to technology often change, and it’s valuable to keep books, especially older ones. “There is also no guarantee that books now available in online databases always will be there,” he said. “Some of the books slated for removal are over 100 years old. Will a pdf still be here in another 100 years? Today's best practice is all too often tomorrow's regret.” He also recalled what some faculty members jokingly called “dumpstergate,” when thousands of books from the Dimond Library were found in a dumpster in 2014. Even though the online collections may be more convenient, Gould said there is value to keeping print books, especially in a public university, since online books are not accessible to a general public that doesn’t have login to large online collections like HathiTrust. “It's hugely important to have those print books available,” he said. “We're a public institution. This is open to the general public and that's a huge part of our mission as a land grant university.” The university is still planning on moving forward with the renovation, but released a FAQ internally to address concerns. The FAQ said the books were selected for review because they hadn’t been checked out in over a decade, and are easily found in another library, or online. “We default to purchasing electronic books rather than print books. We don’t have the budget to purchase more than one copy of a book, so the collection growth is all electronic and has been for the last ten years, since we adopted an e-preferred policy,” the FAQ said. “The print books we own are an increasingly aging and increasingly smaller percentage of our overall collection.” The university is currently reviewing the feedback from faculty, according to the FAQ shared with staff and students.
